extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, literary critics, and students of literature/creative writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for poetic craft, versification, characterization in drama and fiction, and related prose/grammatical concerns as discussed in literary criticism and lectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Milton's rule for poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's definition or rule of poetry: it ought to be simple, sensuous, and impassioned; that is to say, single in conception, abounding in sensible images, and informing them all with the spirit of the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a single overarching conception, saturate the work with concrete, sensory images, and let those images be animated by an intelligent, impassioned perspective. Simplicity of conception combined with rich sensuous detail produces high poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versification, metre, and rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of versification is essential and often neglected; attention to metre and rhythm is prized (Spenser's minute attention to metre and rhythm; good versification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully manage metre, rhythm, rhyme, and lineation; musicality and metrical discipline are core to poetic craft. Minor metrical/rhyme choices (including archaisms) may be allowable when they serve sound and effect (example: debates about 'then/again' vs archaic 'agen'). Neglecting versification is critiqued as a fault in contemporary poets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and metre as core poetic qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: If you take from Virgil his diction and metre, what do you leave him?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction (word choice, phrasing) together with metrical control are central to a poet's distinctiveness; evaluate poetry by how these two interact to produce voice and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausible character psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters' actions should follow from their temperament and the information available to them (example: Othello is not by nature a jealous man; his actions are explainable from the lights he had; Iago's suggestions are new to him).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating or evaluating characters, ensure motivations and reactions are consistent with established disposition and knowledge. Avoid retrofitting traits (e.g., invented 'jealous' predispositions) to justify plot outcomes; plausible psychology increases dramatic credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization through small details ('power in minimis')
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakspeare's power 'in minimis' — the ability to reveal character vividly in very small lines or actions (example: James Gurney's character in King John shown in four words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use compact, sharply drawn moments, gestures, or brief speeches to convey a character's individuality; tiny touches can be decisive in dramatizing personhood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility of dreams versus ghost stories
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a great difference in the credibility to be attached to stories of dreams and stories of ghosts. Dreams can be explained by association, presentiment, or an inner sense; ghost stories are often absurd because real apparitions, when truly believed, produce extreme physical/mental effects, yet many tales leave the seer well afterwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing dreams, exploit associative imagery, inner sense, and subtle presentiment rather than nonsense. When writing supernatural/ghost fiction, respect psychological and physiological consequences (terror, convulsion, madness, death) if the apparition is believed; avoid the anti-pattern of a supposedly terrifying apparition after which the witness is merely fine the next day. Use historical/scriptural (e.g., witch of Endor) or folkloric devices (ventriloquism, trickery) if a naturalistic explanation is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose reflecting authorial persona
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's style in prose is as characteristic of him as a philosophic republican; Latin style may be better than English for certain authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match prose tone, diction, and argumentative stance to the author's intellectual persona and the work's convictions: style should be an expression of viewpoint and character, not merely neutral conveyor of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar and parts-of-speech understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: There are seven parts of speech; inflections of nouns are modifications as to place, inflections of verbs as to time. The genitive denotes dependence; the dative, transmission. Conjunctions are like prepositions prefixed to a sentence or member.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply grammatical knowledge deliberately: know the functions of cases, moods, and inflections to shape meaning and clarity. Avoid loose or incorrect claims about 'verbs governing' without attention to classical usages; precision in grammatical forms supports clarity and stylistic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of rhetorical devices (pun) to clarify
rubrics_metrics.description: A pun will sometimes facilitate explanation (example: 'the Understanding is that which stands under the phenomenon, and gives it objectivity').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ wordplay and rhetorical figures sparingly and purposefully to illuminate abstract concepts; puns can aid explanation when they reveal structural relations, but should not substitute for rigorous argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acoustics and voice in theatrical writing/staging
rubrics_metrics.description: The ancients understood acoustics and contrived to convey the voice distinctly in huge theatres; modern theatres (Drury Lane, Covent Garden) are criticized as too large for acting and too small for a bull-fight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing for the stage or planning performance, consider voice projection, acoustic design, and scale: dialogue and staging must suit the performance space. Practical staging/audibility considerations should inform dramatic writing and production choices.
